Name: analogical_transfer_gate
Title: Solved It Once, Solving It Again: An Internal Analogy Gate That Determines Whether Reasoning Models Reuse a Worked Example or Re-Derive From Scratch
Short Hypothesis: When a reasoning model is shown a fully-worked solution to a structurally-identical problem immediately before the target, it should recognize the shared structure and reuse the method with far less thinking. We hypothesize that reasoning models frequently FAIL to do this, re-deriving from scratch and wasting tokens, and that the difference between transfer and re-derivation is governed by an internal, linearly-decodable 'analogy/structure-mapping' signal that fires (or fails to fire) at the moment the model begins the target problem. Steering this signal causally flips the model between re-derivation and reuse.
Related Work: Two literatures are relevant and previously disconnected. (1) Cognitive science on analogical transfer (Structure-Mapping Theory; 'Transfer Between Analogies', 1995; 'A model of retrieval in problem solving', 1989; 'A theory of relation learning and cross-domain generalization', 2022) documents that humans reuse solutions to structurally-similar problems and characterizes when this transfer succeeds or fails (surface vs. structural similarity, retrieval failures). (2) ML interpretability on circuit and computation reuse (Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks, 2023; Shared Circuits for Sequence Continuation, 2023; Extrapolation by Association, 2025) shows internal components are shared across tasks, and systems work (LLMCache, AttMemo, KVShare, 2023-2025) reuses activations/KV across requests at the infrastructure level. Crucially, NO prior work asks the behavioral question: does a reasoning model behaviorally transfer its OWN just-seen worked solution to a new instance of the same problem, or does it wastefully re-derive? Systems caching reuses computation externally without asking whether the model itself recognizes the analogy; circuit-reuse work studies static shared components, not the dynamic decision to transfer in-context. My prior proposals all concern within-single-problem overthinking; this concerns cross-problem transfer failure and its mechanistic gate. We are the first to (a) quantify in-context analogical-transfer failure in reasoning LLMs, (b) show it is modulated by surface vs. structural similarity as in human analogy, and (c) locate and causally steer an internal analogy gate that switches between reuse and re-derivation.
Abstract: Humans who have just solved a problem reuse the method when they encounter a structurally identical one, thinking far less the second time. We ask whether reasoning language models do the same. We present a reasoning model with a fully-worked solution to a problem, then a target that is structurally identical but differs in surface details (numbers, cover story, variable names), and measure whether the model transfers the method (short, reuse-style reasoning) or re-derives from scratch (long, redundant reasoning). We hypothesize that reasoning models frequently fail to transfer, wasting tokens, and—mirroring human analogy—that transfer succeeds more when surface similarity is high and fails when only deep structure is shared. Across GSM8K, MATH500, and algorithmic word problems on open reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 distills 1.5B-14B, Qwen3), we quantify a transfer-failure rate and its dependence on surface vs. structural similarity. We then test a mechanistic account: at the token boundary where the target problem begins, the residual stream linearly encodes an 'analogy gate' signal predicting whether the model will reuse the worked example or re-derive. We train probes for this signal, test its separability from raw difficulty, localize the carrying components via activation patching (patching the analogy-recognition state from a surface-matched context into a structure-only context), and causally steer the gate to flip reuse vs. re-derivation. Finally we turn the gate into a training-free intervention that induces reuse when a valid analog is present, cutting tokens at equal accuracy. Our work reframes a slice of overthinking as analogical-transfer failure with an identifiable, steerable internal cause.
Experiments: 1) Construct analog pairs: For each seed problem, generate (a) a surface-similar structural analog (same solution method, similar cover story, different numbers), (b) a structure-only analog (same method, different cover story/domain), and (c) a surface-similar but structurally-different distractor (similar wording, different method). Draw seeds from GSM8K, MATH500, and templated algorithmic word problems where the solution method is well-defined. Verify structural equivalence via matching solution-step templates and human/LLM-judge checks. 2) Quantify transfer behavior: Present [worked solution to analog] + [target problem] and measure target reasoning-token count and accuracy, versus a baseline of [target problem alone] and [irrelevant worked solution + target]. Define transfer-success = substantial token reduction with retained accuracy relative to no-analog baseline; transfer-failure = re-derivation (token count similar to no-analog). Metrics: transfer-failure rate, mean token reduction, accuracy, per condition (surface-similar vs structure-only vs distractor). Hypothesis: transfer-failure rate is high overall, lower for surface-similar analogs, higher for structure-only, and the distractor induces harmful reuse (accuracy drop), mirroring human surface-vs-structure effects. 3) Analogy-gate probing (Location): At the token boundary where the target problem begins (after the worked example, before any target reasoning token), extract residual-stream activations. Train per-layer linear probes to predict whether the model will transfer vs. re-derive. Metrics: AUROC/accuracy; layer sweep. Baselines: (i) a difficulty probe (trained on target pass-rate) to test separability from raw difficulty, (ii) surface-similarity feature baseline, (iii) prior-text bag-of-words. Key claim: the gate predicts transfer above and beyond difficulty and surface overlap; test separability via principal angles between gate and difficulty directions. 4) Causal patching: For a fixed target and method, patch the prompt-boundary activation from a surface-similar (transfer-inducing) context into a structure-only (re-derivation) context and measure whether the model switches to reuse (token drop, method-matched solution); report sign, dose, and specificity (matched-random-direction control, off-target accuracy preserved). 5) Gate steering (Causal Intervention): Derive an analogy-gate steering direction (difference-of-means between transfer and re-derivation boundary states). Steer up to induce reuse when a valid analog is present, and steer down as a control. Measure token reduction and accuracy; verify steering does NOT induce harmful reuse of the distractor (specificity). 6) Training-free efficiency application: When a valid worked analog is in context (detected cheaply), apply gate steering to induce reuse. Evaluate tokens-at-equal-accuracy vs no intervention and vs simple prompting ('reuse the method above'). 7) Generalization: transfer probe and steering across datasets and model scales without retraining; test cross-domain analogs (math method reused in a physics word problem).
Risk Factors and Limitations: The analogy gate may be inseparable from raw difficulty or surface-overlap features, weakening the mechanistic claim; the separability analysis, patching, and distractor-specificity tests directly address this, and a null would still yield a novel behavioral characterization of transfer failure. Constructing clean structural analogs that hold difficulty constant while varying surface similarity is nontrivial; we mitigate with template-based generation and human/LLM verification of structural equivalence. Transfer-success detection relies on token-count and method-match, which are noisy; we use both token-reduction and step-template matching and validate with human spot-checks. Inducing reuse could cause harmful transfer to structurally-different distractors (accuracy loss); the distractor condition and steering-specificity metric quantify this trade-off. Reasoning-length measurement requires clear think/answer delimiters. Effects and the strength of surface-vs-structure modulation may be model-family and scale specific, and cross-domain transfer may be rare in smaller models (itself an informative result).
